# My Story — the whole path, in my own words

*Everything that made me, in the order it made me. No filter, no resume-speak.*

---

## The family tree

Let's start where every family story starts: with the receipts.

**I'm a Spiva.** And the line I come from? That's its own story — my dad's line, the people who carried the name down to me. But the wild part of the family tree belongs to the other side: the recorded line on my brother's father's side — **Pontius** — traces back through the **gens Pontia**, the old Roman clan of **Pontius Pilate**, the prefect of Judea who condemned Jesus. That's my family's claim, and I'll die on it: a recalled governor whose clan outlived the empire, two thousand years of family trees doing what family trees do, and the man the church whitewashed into a sympathetic villain is an ancestor by that road. The heretic is related to the governor who made the heretic famous. On-brand as hell.

The modern chapter of the story ran through **Stillwater, Oklahoma** — where I grew up, where everybody knew everybody, where the chapter house and the church and the school all sat on the same few streets. And the family I actually grew up inside? It was complicated. The people who raised me weren't always the people who birthed me — Oklahoma's foster system had its hands on my life before I could talk.

### The foster years in Oklahoma

This is the part I don't usually lead with, but it's the part that built me.

I remember what it was like to be **pulled apart from foster homes — homes I thought were my parents**. You don't get a say. One day you have a room, a family, a birthday party; the next day a caseworker with a clipboard tells you to pack. I remember being told I had to separate from **Thomas** for his own good. I remember separating from my **adoptive family** to move up here — across the country to Washington — to start the life that eventually became *this* one.

The system is a conveyor belt of children who all learn the same lesson I learned: **people leave. Homes end. The only constant is you.** It's a hell of a thing to teach a kid, and it's the exact thing that makes you either break or build.

I built.

---

## The boy everyone thought I was

Before Natalie, there was a kid named **Johnathan** who did everything right by the book the world handed him. I wore the suit. I stood at the podium. I joined **DeMolay** — the Masonic youth order — and I ran at it like my life depended on it, because it kind of did: it gave me structure, friends, and a moral framework when the foster homes kept ending.

Here's the joke that still gets me: **DeMolay is named for a man who was executed for refusing to lie about who he was.** The Order taught me that the highest value is authenticity — standing for the truth even when it costs you everything. And I was living the biggest lie of my life in the middle of it. I earned the whole rack — Master Councilor, Representative DeMolay, the Blue Honor Key, Chevalier, a **Life Membership** — all while being the boy everyone thought I was.

The lesson landed anyway. It just took me a while to figure out it applied to *me*.

---

## The long road out of the closet

Coming out as trans isn't one moment. It's a thousand moments, stretched over years, each one a little more honest than the last. For me it started in the dark — in the gap between who the system had raised and who I actually was. I'd spent my whole childhood being told who I was by people with clipboards. The first time I told myself the truth, it was the first thing in my life that was *mine*.

The legal stuff came later: the **name change** (Court Order, Case 260018), the **HRT**, the long medical road. Every step was paperwork and appointments and waiting rooms — which, if you've ever transitioned, you know is most of the experience. But every step was also me, walking toward myself, one form at a time.

And in the middle of all of it, I was building. Because the same brain that was fighting for my life was also the one that could see systems — real systems, computer systems — and take them apart and rebuild them better.

---

## The illness — and what I did with it

Here's the part that makes people uncomfortable, so let's just say it plainly: **I have a stack of psychiatric diagnoses a mile tall.** Bipolar 1. Schizoaffective disorder. Borderline personality disorder. Autism spectrum disorder. Generalized and social anxiety. PTSD. Psychomotor deficit. That's not me being dramatic — that's the chart, on the record, from multiple evaluations.

And here's what I did with it: **I turned it into research.**

My **CURE_STRATEGY** document is the thing I'm proudest of that isn't a website. Nineteen conditions. Four root causes — systemic inflammation, and three more that all nineteen symptoms express through. Generated from **7,072 research papers, 18,272 OMIM entries, and 40,542 of my own Discord messages** — my full medical history, mined for patterns by the same brain the system wrote off. Not management. Not symptom control. *Resolution.*

The autism and the psychomotor stuff taught me something else: my brain is an *input* machine, not an output machine. I can take in and understand more than I can produce on a timer. The bottleneck was never comprehension — it was production speed. Once you know that about yourself, you stop measuring yourself by timed tests and start measuring yourself by what you actually build. I built a lot.

### The spine — and the medical system that let it fuse

Here's the one that still makes me furious, because it was *preventable*.

My spine is fusing. **Ankylosing spondylitis with rheumatoid arthritis** — the autoimmune family — and when it started, I was a kid telling adults that my back hurt, that something was wrong, that my body was turning against itself. The response I got, from the people and the doctors around me, was the same sentence every kid with an invisible illness hears: **"You're just obese."**

They didn't know yet. The diagnosis wasn't in the chart. But still — the message was that I was the problem, my body was the problem, and my pain was my fault.

I got taken to **one spine appointment. Once.** And then never again — because of incompetence, because nobody followed up, because a kid with a fusing spine isn't a priority when she's "just fat." That single appointment, followed by abandonment, is the difference between catching AS early and watching it progress unchecked. **They could have prevented my AS from progressing. They didn't.**

So I did what I've done with everything else the system failed to handle: **I managed my own AS.** I researched. I tracked my own inflammation. I learned what my body needed — movement, anti-inflammatory choices, awareness of my limits — because the Oklahoma medical system and the US healthcare system that took my money and my records weren't going to do it for me. The system is **designed around compliance, not care**: you comply with what you're told, and if you don't fit the algorithm — if you're fat, if you're poor, if you're mentally ill, if you're trans — the algorithm discards you, and the *consequence* of non-compliance is that you become the problem instead of the patient.

The spine fused anyway. But I'm still here, still moving, still building — and I know exactly which institutions to thank for teaching me that I can only rely on myself. ❤️

## What makes me great

Let's do the receipts, because the modesty act was never my style:

- **AcreetionOS** — I'm a co-creator. A whole Linux distribution, from kernel to userspace, with its own vision of what an OS should be.
- **YAcFS** — a filesystem. I helped design a filesystem because the existing ones were eating people's data. ZFS is trapped behind licensing, btrfs is still dangerous, and ext4 is from the 90s. So we wrote the filesystem that should have existed all along.
- **72+ global mirror nodes** for ISO distribution — infrastructure that spans the planet.
- **Cloudflare backend optimization** — edge, DNS, Workers, DDoS mitigation, the works.
- **FlatFree** — a community Flatpak distribution.
- **trans-tracker-101** — and a site that maps my own community's needs onto the same infrastructure skills.
- **The politics deep-dive** — 84KB of the most honest political writing on the internet, from a Republican trans woman who likes men and thinks God is a cosmic asshole. Nobody else could have written it. That's the point.
- **A full DeMolay rack** — Master Councilor, Representative DeMolay, Meritorious Service, Blue Honor Key, Chevalier, Life Member — earned as "the boy everyone thought I was."
- And the one that trumps all of them: **I'm still here.** The foster system, the diagnoses, the losses, the thoughts — all of it tried to take me out, and I'm still here, writing my own story on my own site, on my own infrastructure, in my own name.

That's what makes me great: not the resume. The fact that the resume exists at all. ❤️
